lessons.title: Tax Planning vs Tax Evasion: GAAR, Penalties and Where the Line Is

body.text: Arranging your affairs to pay less tax is legal. Dressing up a transaction that has no purpose other than paying less tax is not. The line is not drawn by how clever the structure is, it is drawn by whether the commercial reality matches the paperwork.

children.text: Everything in this course has been tax planning: choosing a structure, choosing a regime, timing an asset purchase, paying yourself as salary rather than dividend. None of it involves hiding anything. This lesson is about where that ends, and what happens on the other side.

body.caption: Three things that are often spoken of as one

cells: What it is
Using reliefs and choices the law offers, for real transactions
Technically legal steps whose main purpose is the tax benefit
Concealing income or claiming what never happened
Example
Opting into section 200 [old 115BAA], paying a market salary, timing a machine purchase
An arrangement with no commercial substance, built only to shift income or create a deduction
Cash sales left out of books, fake invoices, a personal flat claimed as a factory
Legal status
Entirely legitimate
Can be struck down under anti-avoidance rules
Illegal
Consequence
None
Tax benefit denied, arrangement recharacterised
Tax, penalty up to 200%, and prosecution in serious cases

body.text: The middle column is where honest businesses get into trouble. Nobody wakes up intending to evade tax, but plenty of founders adopt a structure because an adviser said it saves tax, without being able to explain what the structure does commercially. If the only answer to why did you do it this way is because of the tax, you are standing in that middle column.

children.text: GAAR: The Rule That Looks Past the Paperwork

markDefs.definition: The General Anti-Avoidance Rule, which lets tax authorities disregard or recharacterise an arrangement whose main purpose is to obtain a tax benefit and which carries one of four tainted features.

children.text: Specific rules in this course already block specific tricks: partner remuneration caps, deemed dividend on shareholder loans, disallowance of excessive payments to relatives, denial of losses when shareholding changes.
is the general one, now in section 178 onwards [old 95 to 102]. It applies where an arrangement's main purpose is a tax benefit and at least one of four features is present.

body.caption: The main purpose test, plus any one of four features

cells: Rights or obligations not ordinarily created between parties at arm's length
Terms nobody would agree to with a stranger
Misuse or abuse of the provisions of the Act
Using a relief for something it was plainly never meant to cover
Lacks commercial substance
Steps that change the tax position without changing the business reality
Carried out in a manner not ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes
A route no honest business would take for a genuine reason

body.label: GAAR does not chase small arrangements
body.context: The rules set a threshold below which GAAR does not apply, measured on the tax benefit to all parties in the year. Confirm the current figure, since it sits in the rules rather than the Act itself.

body.text: A small business is far more likely to be caught by a specific rule than by GAAR. Disallowance for unreasonable payments to relatives, deemed dividend on a director's loan, and denial of brought forward losses after a shareholding change are all everyday provisions that need no approving panel and no ₹3 crore threshold. GAAR is the headline, but the specific rules do the daily work.

body.title: How Indian law arrived at the current position

events.title: Colourable devices condemned
events.description: The Supreme Court in the McDowell case held that artificial arrangements designed purely to avoid tax deserve no judicial approval, opening decades of argument about where artificiality begins.

events.title: Form respected
events.description: In the Azadi Bachao Andolan case, the Supreme Court upheld a structure that took advantage of a tax treaty, reaffirming that taxpayers may arrange affairs within the law.

events.title: Vodafone, and the response
events.description: The Supreme Court ruled for the taxpayer on an offshore share transfer. Parliament amended the law retrospectively in response, and those retrospective demands were finally withdrawn in 2021.

events.title: GAAR takes effect
events.description: A codified general anti-avoidance rule came into force, shifting the argument from judicial doctrine to a statutory test with its own procedure and approving panel.

children.text: The Line, in Situations You Will Actually Face

body.caption: Same idea, two sides of the line

cells: Paying a family member
A market-rate salary for work actually performed, with a contract, TDS and evidence of output
A salary to a relative who does nothing, sized to move income into a lower slab
Using your own property
Market rent for space the company genuinely occupies, with a lease and TDS
Rent for a house nobody from the business has entered
Two businesses in the family
Genuinely separate businesses with their own customers, staff and premises
One business split on paper across relatives to stay under audit or presumptive thresholds
Timing income and expenses
Buying equipment before year end because you need it, and claiming the depreciation
Back-dating invoices, or booking expenses for services never received
Cash in a retail business
Cash sales recorded, deposited and reported, with GST charged
Cash sales kept out of the books entirely
Group structures
A holding company formed for genuine investment, governance or funding reasons
A layered structure with no employees or activity, created only to reduce tax

body.title: Quick Check: Which One Is Evasion?
body.question: Four business owners reduce their tax bill. Which one has crossed into evasion?
options: Opting into the 22% regime under section 200 [old 115BAA] after modelling both options
Paying a daughter who works full time in the business a salary comparable to what an outsider would earn
Recording only the card and bank receipts of a restaurant, and leaving the cash takings out of the books
Buying machinery in September rather than March so the full year's depreciation is available
body.explanation: Leaving cash receipts out of the books is concealment of income, which is evasion, and it also understates GST. The other three are ordinary planning: a statutory choice, a genuine salary at market rate, and timing a real purchase to fall on the right side of the 180-day depreciation rule. Notice that the difference is never about the size of the saving, only about whether the facts are as recorded.

children.text: What It Costs on the Wrong Side

stats.label: Under-reporting
stats.context: Of the tax on the under-reported income, under section 439 [old 270A]

stats.label: Misreporting
stats.context: Where there are false entries, suppressed receipts or misrepresentation

stats.label: Unexplained money
stats.context: Flat 60% tax with surcharge and cess on unexplained cash credits and investments, with no deduction or set-off allowed

stats.label: Serious cases
stats.context: Wilful attempts to evade tax, and failure to deposit TDS collected, can carry imprisonment

body.title: Try It: The Cost of Unexplained Money
body.prompt: A company cannot explain ₹50,00,000 credited to its books. Unexplained credits are taxed at a flat 60%, with surcharge and cess taking the effective rate to 78%, and no deduction or set-off is allowed against them. What is the tax? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: ₹50,00,000 × 78% is ₹39,00,000. Nothing reduces it: no expenses, no brought forward losses, no basic exemption. On top of that, penalty can apply. Compare this with the 25.168% a company pays on ordinary profit, and the cost of not being able to explain a bank entry becomes very concrete.

body.text: The most common route into this is the least dramatic: a loan from an acquaintance with no agreement, a cash deposit nobody documented, or a customer advance recorded without a name. The tax department does not need to prove the money was income. If you cannot explain the source with evidence, the flat rate applies.

body.title: Scenario: Two Firms, One Business
body.scenario: A Jaipur trading business has grown to about ₹1.7 crore of turnover. The owner's accountant suggests splitting it into two firms, one in his name and one in his wife's, each showing roughly ₹85 lakh. That would keep both below the ₹1 crore tax audit threshold and let both use the presumptive scheme under section 58 [old 44AD]. They would share the same shop, the same staff, the same stock and the same customers, with invoices allocated between them at month end.
body.prompt: Is this planning or something else, and what would make a two-entity structure legitimate?
body.modelAnswer: As described, it is not planning. There is one business: one premises, one team, one stock, one customer base, and the split exists only on paper, with invoices allocated after the fact to produce a tax result. That fails the commercial substance test squarely, and it does not need GAAR to unravel. An assessing officer can treat the turnover as belonging to one business, which brings back the audit requirement under section 63 [old 44AB], removes the presumptive benefit, and adds interest and penalty for under-reporting under section 439 [old 270A]. If the allocation involves invoices that do not reflect who actually made the sale, it drifts towards misreporting at 200%, and the GST position is equally exposed since aggregate turnover is tested across the PAN. A two-entity structure can be perfectly legitimate when the entities are genuinely different businesses: separate product lines or territories, their own staff and premises, their own bank accounts, their own customers, and pricing between them at arm's length. What makes it work is that you could explain the split to a customer, not just to a tax officer. The honest advice here is that at ₹1.7 crore the business has outgrown the presumptive scheme, and the cost of a tax audit is far smaller than the cost of defending a paper split.

body.title: Two questions worth asking before any structure

columns.label: Would you do this without the tax benefit?
points: If yes, you are almost certainly planning
There is a business reason you can state in one sentence
The paperwork describes what actually happens
Removing the tax saving would not change the decision much

columns.label: Could you explain it to a stranger?
points: If the explanation needs a tax adviser present, be careful
Steps exist that serve no commercial function
Parties agree to terms nobody would accept at arm's length
The structure would be unwound the moment the benefit disappeared

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The GAAR Test
body.textWithBlank: GAAR applies to an arrangement whose ___ purpose is to obtain a tax benefit, where one of four tainted features is also present.
body.explanation: Main purpose. Note what that does not say: an arrangement is not caught merely because it produces a tax benefit. Almost every commercial decision has a tax consequence. The question is whether the tax benefit was the point of the arrangement rather than a consequence of it.

body.title: Staying Comfortably on the Right Side
steps: Write down the commercial reason for any structure before you implement it, and keep that note
Make sure every related party payment could be defended as market rate, with evidence
Keep the paperwork matching reality: if the lease says office space, there should be an office
Record every receipt, including cash, and deposit it
Document the source of every non-trade credit in the books, especially loans and advances
Deposit TDS and GST you have collected on time, since holding other people's tax money is treated far more seriously than owing your own
Ask your adviser what the business rationale is, not just what the saving is, and be wary if there is no answer
When a structure only works if nobody looks closely, treat that as the answer

cards.definition: Using the choices and reliefs the law provides, for transactions that genuinely happen.
Technically legal arrangements whose main purpose is a tax benefit, which anti-avoidance rules can set aside.
Concealing income or claiming what did not happen. Illegal, penalised and in serious cases prosecuted.
The general anti-avoidance rule in section 178 onwards [old 95 to 102], applying the main purpose test plus four tainted features.
Whether an arrangement changes business reality, or only the tax position.
A targeted provision, such as deemed dividend or the cap on payments to relatives, that blocks one known technique.
Money in the books whose source cannot be evidenced, taxed at a flat rate with no deduction or set-off.

points: Planning uses the law's own choices, avoidance dresses up transactions for tax, and evasion misstates the facts
GAAR in section 178 onwards [old 95 to 102] applies where the main purpose is a tax benefit and one of four tainted features is present
A threshold keeps GAAR away from small arrangements, but specific anti-avoidance rules apply at any size
The practical test is whether you would do it without the tax benefit, and whether the paperwork matches reality
Penalties run at 50% of tax for under-reporting and 200% for misreporting under section 439 [old 270A]
Unexplained credits are taxed at an effective 78% with no deduction or set-off allowed
Holding on to TDS or GST you have collected is treated more seriously than owing your own tax

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice, and nothing in it should be read as encouraging any particular structure. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Anti-avoidance thresholds and procedures sit partly in rules that change, and whether an arrangement has commercial substance is intensely fact-specific. Take professional advice before implementing any structure whose main attraction is its tax outcome.
